items.title: The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron enforced the 1807 ban
items.claim: How was the 1807 abolition of the British slave trade enforced?

options.text: By voluntary compliance from British merchants only

The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron (formed 1808, based at Sierra Leone) intercepted slave ships off the African coast; by the 1860s it had captured around 1,600 ships and freed around 150,000 enslaved Africans
By signing treaties with no enforcement mechanism
By immediately ending all transatlantic shipping

items.reveal:
The West Africa Squadron began with two ships and grew to around 25 by mid-century — about a sixth of the Royal Navy. Captures were brought before Vice-Admiralty courts at Freetown; freed Africans were resettled in Sierra Leone or recruited as 'Liberated African' sailors.

The squadron's mortality rate was very high — yellow fever, malaria, and combat. By the 1840s, treaties with Portugal, Spain and others widened the squadron's powers.

The US South continued importing enslaved people illegally until the Civil War, but the Atlantic trade was largely suppressed by the 1860s. Brazil — the last major importer — banned the trade in 1850 and abolished slavery in 1888.
items.why: Abolishing a trade is different from enforcing the ban. Britain's commitment of naval power for over 60 years made 1807 effective — and reframed the slave trade as an international policing problem.

items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.

items.title: Edward Jenner did not invent inoculation
items.claim: What did Edward Jenner demonstrate in 1796?

options.text: The first prevention of smallpox in human history
That deliberate infection with cowpox (vaccinia) protected against smallpox — a safer alternative to existing variolation (deliberate infection with smallpox itself)
That smallpox could be cured after infection

items.reveal:
Variolation — inoculation with smallpox itself — was practised in China, India, the Ottoman Empire and West Africa centuries before Jenner. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to Britain from Constantinople in 1721. It worked but killed around 1-2% of those treated.

Jenner's experiment on 14 May 1796 used pus from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes's cowpox sores, inoculated into 8-year-old James Phipps. Phipps was later challenged with smallpox and did not become ill.

Jenner published in 1798. The Vaccination Act 1853 made it compulsory in England. WHO declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980.
items.why: The 'lone genius' narrative misses preceding practice. Jenner improved a known technique with a safer biological substitute — major progress, but not the first prevention.
